name: Bill Gates
role: Co-founder of Microsoft (1975); chair of the Gates Foundation; philanthropist and energy investor (Breakthrough Energy, TerraPower)
summary: Gates is a technology-optimist philanthropist who favours using market incentives, public research funding and government aid to reduce global health and poverty gaps. He has argued that the rich should pay higher taxes, backs nuclear power and clean-energy innovation while arguing since 2025 that climate policy should centre on human welfare, and supports rich-country aid, GM crops and strong intellectual property. Recorded views on social, cultural, constitutional and security questions are sparse.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Credits capitalism with harnessing self-interest to drive innovation, but says market incentives leave the poorest unserved and that governments, philanthropy and policy must steer markets; mixed record, not a clear agree or disagree.

public-ownership.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 11) describes the government-owned PTT telephone monopolies abroad as slow and the regulated monopolies as producing limited innovation, and calls for deregulation and competition in telecommunications. This is about one utility sector only.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Wrote in 2020 that the rich, himself included, should pay more, urged higher estate and capital-gains taxes, and said the top 1% can pay a lot more without losing incentive; supported Washington's state income tax.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Chapters 10 and 11 call for emissions rules, clean electricity and fuel standards and updated regulations on companies, though in 1998 Senate testimony he rejected regulating the software industry. Evidence is mixed by sector.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Said that with safeguards there are cases where government action such as stopping terrorism is valuable, and floated 'benign surveillance' of laboratories to stop bioterror, while warning of past abuses.

state-harmful.rationale: Repeatedly says government must act (education, research, aid, health, taxes): 'Only the government has the resources to effect change on a broad scale.'

same-sex-marriage.rationale: In 2012 he gave $100,000 and then $500,000 (with Melinda) to the campaign to approve Washington State's same-sex marriage law in Referendum 74.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Testified for lifting the H-1B cap and more green cards for skilled workers; his documented position concerns skilled immigration only.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Funds and champions multilateral bodies (Gavi, Global Fund, WHO-linked work) and in his Aug 2026 AI essay proposed a new international body modeled on nuclear inspection and aviation regulation.

free-trade.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 12) says the network will spur international trade in intellectual goods and services and produce a wealthier, more stable world. In 2019 he opposed a zero-sum trade conflict with China and in 2025 said tariffs bring no benefit and hurt poor countries.

nation-first.rationale: Urges rich countries including the US to keep funding global health and calls for global cooperation on AI and health.

limit-growth.rationale: Argues for innovation and prosperity as the answer to climate change rather than limiting growth; says 'health and prosperity' are the best defense and wants poor countries to grow.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Backs major government action (R&D, mandates, subsidies, carbon pricing, praised the Inflation Reduction Act), but his Oct 2025 memo rejects a 'doomsday view' and stresses welfare and adaptation, so 'drastic' is only partly matched.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Describes himself as an impatient optimist who saw 'breakthroughs in technology could solve key problems', while stressing that technology alone leaves the poor behind without policy and system change.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Founded and chairs TerraPower to build safe, clean next-generation nuclear; said wind and solar need 'a storage miracle or ... nuclear fission or fusion'.

central-planning.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 11 and ch. 6) says that in an unproven market, many companies trying different approaches reach the right answer much faster than any form of central planning, and that governments cannot outsmart the competitive marketplace.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Called for raising the estate tax in his 2020 blog post; the degree ('heavily') is not stated in the sources opened.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In May 2025 he said the Trump tariff plan creates uncertainty that discourages investment, would hurt poor countries, and that he saw no benefit in it; in 2019 he said the US-China tariff conflict has few winners.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Urged governments to fund clean-energy R&D and, in 2020, to create federal energy research institutes; this is public R&D funding rather than steering investment into named strategic industries, so ambiguous.

direct-votes.rationale: In The Road Ahead (ch. 12) he says he does not think direct voting is a good way to run a government: representatives add value by mastering complicated issues and by making the compromises that politics needs.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Wants more progressive taxes and mobility but stresses keeping the incentive to dream and invent; focuses on opportunity rather than equal results.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Says 'the world is getting better, a lot better' and calls the technology-driven period a high point in human welfare.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Mixed: The Road Ahead (ch. 12) welcomes rapid change but says society should not take hasty action; in 2017 he proposed taxing robots to slow the pace of automation somewhat, and in 2026 he proposed taxes and reserved jobs to manage AI's effect.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: In the 2016 Apple/FBI dispute he said that with the right safeguards government access can be valuable and 'you want to strike that balance', while not endorsing a general back door.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Criticized an 'ideological wedge' over biotechnology and stresses measuring impact and relying on evidence.

taxation-theft.rationale: In The Road Ahead (ch. 12) he described taxes as how high earners pay more for roads, schools, the army and other services and said he had no complaint about paying over $100 million; in 2019 he said he would accept paying far more.

reason-over-faith.rationale: In a 2014 Rolling Stone interview he said it makes sense to believe in God and that religion's moral systems are important, which does not fit the claim that reason alone should guide knowledge and action.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Divested from fossil fuels (2019), backs net-zero emissions, a green premium of zero and a tax disadvantaging the dirty option; has not addressed expanding domestic production directly.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Wrote that 'left to their own devices, systems often leave women behind', and makes gender equality an underpinning of foundation work.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Chapter 10 says that for massive undertakings such as highways, vaccinating the world's children or decarbonizing the economy the government must play a huge role, and he regrets earlier avoiding policy makers.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Says 'every life has equal value' and finds it revolting that some lives are seen as worth saving and others not.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Frames reducing inequity as the highest human achievement and directs the foundation to the poorest; 'first priority' in law and institutions is not his wording.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Criticizes aid cuts by the US and others, says polio will not be eradicated without US funding, and calls on governments to partner on global health; accused Musk of harming the world's poorest children over USAID cuts.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Supports 'a tax system in which, if you have more money, you pay a higher percentage in taxes'.

ban-cartels.rationale: Mixed: The Road Ahead (ch. 11) says governments should assure a strong competitive framework and open monopolized telecom markets, but a federal court found Microsoft guilty of monopolization in the 1990s case, which he contested and later called a distraction.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Chapter 11 says governments can refuse trade agreements and partnerships with countries that have not taken climate change seriously, and can apply carbon border adjustments, with allowances for low-income countries.

delink-world-market.rationale: Wants businesses in poor countries to reach rich-world markets (e.g. African coffee farmers) and wants market forces extended to the poor.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Chapter 6 calls plant-based meat a huge boon for animal welfare when fewer livestock are kept in small cages.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Chapter 6 rejects ending livestock as unrealistic because meat is central to culture, while backing alternatives that cut livestock numbers and improve welfare.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Endorsed Carnegie's view that the wealthy have a duty to return resources to society, cites his mother's 'to whom much is given much is expected', and pledged to give away virtually all his wealth.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Argues poor countries need outside funding, innovation and market access; notes African governments are stepping up but it is 'still not enough'.

local-production.rationale: Chapter 7 (How We Get Around) welcomes year-round fruit shipped from South America and wants shipping decarbonized rather than food production relocalized.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: In The Road Ahead (ch. 9) he proposes government-funded curricula available free while private vendors, other public schools and teachers compete to improve them, and says the network would increase choice in schooling. This is education only.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Says capitalism's genius is making self-interest serve the wider interest and that it is responsible for innovations that improved many lives.

social-market-economy.rationale: Notes that nearly every country is capitalist and that the Nordic countries do well on the safety net and opportunity; says the system can be more progressive without killing aspiration.

online-participation.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 12) predicts that the network will become a primary conduit of political discourse, that voters could cast ballots from home with less fraud, and that it will make organizing political movements easy, and he presents these developments positively.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Said voluntary giving 'is not a scalable solution' and that charity cannot replace taxes; says no philanthropy can fill the gap left by government aid cuts.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: He names pandemics and bioterrorism, nuclear war and keeping control of AI as the very scary risks, warned in 2024 that the world has not learned from COVID-19, and in 2026 called for government regulation and oversight of AI because misuse could cause 'a billion deaths'. He has not framed it as extinction risk as such.

abolish-ip.rationale: Opposed the COVID-19 vaccine TRIPS waiver and argued patents were not the bottleneck; his career built on software intellectual property.

online-anonymity.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 8) notes that anonymous posting leaves little accountability in unmoderated forums and says ways must be found to curb abusive posts, though it does not propose banning pseudonyms.

gm-crops.rationale: Told the 2009 World Food Prize forum that GM crops are important tools and criticized restricting biotechnology in Africa; the foundation funds GM and biofortified crops.

dense-cities.rationale: Chapter 10 lists zoning that raises density so people travel less between work and home as a tool cities can use to cut emissions.

free-public-college.rationale: Asked 'Why should college be free?' and called it a regressive upper-class idea because middle-class taxpayers would fund students likely to earn a lot.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Described a tax that disadvantages the dirty approach as one of several policy tools (after innovation, requirements and subsidies); also reported to urge carbon pricing in his 2021 book.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The Road Ahead (ch. 11) criticizes government-granted monopolies and exclusive franchises in telecommunications and cable as curbing competition and innovation, and urges deregulation. The statement is about privileges for connected firms generally.

automate-paid-work.rationale: His 2026 essay proposes a tax on AI tokens and robots and a set of jobs reserved for humans, and in 2017 he wanted to slow automation; he does link larger reserved shares to possible shorter workweeks, which leaves it short of strong disagreement.

notes:
Replaced an old pilot audit. Gates Notes pages were blocked for direct download; his own words come from the Gates Foundation republication of his 2025 essay, a Wayback copy of the 2023 AI essay, speeches, and podcast transcripts, while his 2020 tax post, Oct 2025 climate memo, 2016 encryption remarks and 2008 testimony are known through quoting reports or Microsoft's release. Where views changed, the recent position was used (2025 climate memo; AI essay of Aug 2026 reported by Wikipedia). All other statements are null: no inference from his wealth or industry.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 8 answers taken from it, 18 agreed, 1 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Book dates from 2021; later positions (2025 memo says climate is not an existential threat and stresses health and poverty priorities, while he still backs emissions cuts and clean-energy spending) do not change the answers. His 2016 remarks on FBI v. Apple were disputed and not used. Healthcare, abortion and other social items left null for lack of a clear stated position.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 15 answers taken from it, 25 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: The Road Ahead (1995) is the main primary source here, covering government, privacy, encryption, education, jobs, taxes, representation and markets. Where later statements differ, the later one is used: climate emphasis (2025 memo), AI regulation (2026), and tax views (2019). Gates's own Gates Notes and foundation pages returned 403 or 404, so later positions rest on press reports of his interviews and speeches, capped at the confidence those allow. Left null where only a general principle or a nearby topic was found: universal healthcare, vouchers, unions, minimum wage, guns (he funded a background-check initiative, which is narrower than strict limits), abortion, drugs, policing, death penalty.
